result.summary: Achilles and the Myrmidons mourn Patroclus, whose ghost appears and asks for burial. The pyre is built and lit with the help of the winds, and the bones are gathered. Achilles then holds funeral games: chariot race, boxing, wrestling, running, armed combat, quoit, archery and javelin.

scenes.title: Mourning beside the ships
scenes.summary: Achilles leads the Myrmidons in lament round Patroclus, vows to give Hector to the dogs, and refuses to wash until the burial. He falls asleep on the shore.
scenes.stakes: Achilles is consumed by grief and cannot rest until Patroclus is properly buried.

place.name: the Achaean camp by the Hellespont

scenes.title: The ghost of Patroclus
scenes.summary: Patroclus's spirit asks Achilles for swift burial and for their bones to share one urn. Achilles tries to embrace him but the ghost vanishes.
scenes.stakes: Patroclus cannot enter Hades until buried; Achilles faces his own foretold death.

scenes.title: Wood gathered and the pyre built
scenes.summary: Meriones leads the wood-gathering on Ida. Achilles gives his lock to Patroclus and builds the pyre, sacrificing animals and twelve Trojans. Venus and Apollo protect Hector's body.
scenes.stakes: Hector's body is threatened with desecration; Achilles' rage drives his sacrifices.

place.name: Mount Ida and the shore at Troy

scenes.title: The winds light the pyre
scenes.summary: The pyre will not burn, so Achilles prays to Boreas and Zephyrus. Iris fetches them and they blow all night. At dawn the bones are gathered in a golden urn and a mound is raised.
scenes.stakes: Without the fire, Patroclus cannot be released to the dead.

scenes.title: The chariot race
scenes.summary: Five drivers race. Apollo and Minerva intervene, Diomed wins, and Antilochus beats Menelaus by a trick but yields the mare. Achilles consoles Eumelus and honours Nestor.
scenes.stakes: Antilochus risks his honour and a prize; Menelaus risks being thought a cheat.

place.name: the plain by the ships at Troy

scenes.title: Boxing and wrestling
scenes.summary: Epeus knocks out Euryalus in the boxing. Ajax and Ulysses wrestle to a draw and share the prize.
scenes.stakes: Competitors risk injury and pride for the prizes.

scenes.title: Running, arms, quoit, archery, javelin
scenes.summary: Ulysses wins the foot-race with Minerva's help. Ajax and Diomed fight to a draw, Polypoetes wins the quoit, Meriones wins the archery, and Agamemnon is honoured without throwing.
scenes.stakes: Competitors seek prizes and honour; Teucer loses for neglecting Apollo.

notable_quotes.reason: Patroclus' ghost reproaches the sleeping Achilles, a moving ghost scene.
Achilles voices that there is a time to mourn and a time to stop.

analysis.text: Grief gives way to ritual and communal order. Achilles' rage at Hector persists, but the games show him as a generous, fair leader.
The passage reflects Homeric funeral customs: cremation, a mound, ashes in an urn, and athletic contests honouring the dead, and human sacrifice.

legacy.text: The funeral games of Patroclus became the model for epic funeral games, notably in Virgil's Aeneid Book 5.

fun_facts.text: Nestor's advice about the turning post is a classic ancient lesson that skill beats raw speed.

language_notes.text: "Forsooth" is an archaic word meaning 'in truth' or 'indeed'; here it adds a slightly formal, emphatic tone.
"A minister of fear" means a cause or bringer of fear to enemies: Patroclus was a formidable warrior, so his loss is wept over so heavily.
"Contumely" means insulting, contemptuous treatment. Achilles is dishonouring Hector's corpse.
"Fleet descendant of Aeacus" is a way of naming Achilles; his grandfather was Aeacus.
"The flames of Vulcan" means simply fire; Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus) is the god of fire and the forge.
"Meet" means proper or fitting; "barrow" is a burial mound; "nigh" means near.
The dead could not enter Hades until the body received funeral rites; unburied, Patroclus is stuck outside, barred by the other ghosts from crossing the river.
"Dues of fire" means the rites of cremation owed to the dead. After the pyre, the spirit cannot return to the living.
"Take sweet counsel" means to talk and plan intimately together, as friends who share their thoughts.
Patroclus recalls killing a boy in a quarrel over dice as a child, which led his father Menoetius to send him into exile with Peleus.
"Squire" renders the attendant or comrade who served a warrior; here Patroclus became Achilles' companion and helper.
"Rosy-fingered morn" is the standard Homeric formula for dawn.
"Up hill and down dale" means over all kinds of terrain, rough and smooth; the doubled phrase stresses the length of the journey.
"Monument" here means the burial mound (barrow) to be raised over the ashes, not a statue.
Cutting and laying locks of hair on the dead was a Greek mourning custom, offering part of oneself to the departed.
A hecatomb was properly a sacrifice of a hundred oxen; here it is used loosely for a great offering, fifty goats.
"Give ear" means listen to and obey; Achilles acknowledges Agamemnon's authority over the army.
"Vaunt" means to boast; Achilles' threat to Hector's body proves empty.
Boreas is the north wind and Zephyrus the west wind; the Greeks treated winds as gods who could be addressed and bribed.
"Boisterous" means rough and noisy, a fitting epithet for a wind god's household.
Hecatombs are large sacrifices of cattle, originally a hundred, offered to the gods.
"Achaeans" is Homer's common name for the Greeks as a whole.
"Bridegroom son" means a newly married son, which makes the parents' loss sharper.
"Suffuse" means spread over; the Morning Star appears just before sunrise, announcing the dawn.
The bones are wrapped in fat for preservation until Achilles' own death, when they will be buried together.
A barrow is an earthen burial mound.
"Swart" means dark or black; here it describes iron, a valuable metal in the Homeric world.
"Ears for handles" refers to the loop handles on either side of the cauldron.
A talent was a measured weight of gold, used as a unit of value.
Refers to an earlier battle in which Diomed captured Aeneas' horses, and Apollo carried the wounded Aeneas away.
Echepolus bought his way out of military service by giving Agamemnon the mare, so he could stay in wealthy Sicyon instead of going to Troy (Ilius).
The sentence is awkwardly built: it contrasts the driver who swings wide with the skilled one who, though his horses are worse, keeps control at the turn.
The "nave" is the hub of the wheel; Nestor wants it to nearly brush the turning post.
Arion, a divinely bred horse, belonged to Adrastus (here Adrestus); Laomedon's horses were famed Trojan stock. Nestor names them as the fastest imaginable.
"Descendant of Pheres" is a patronymic for Eumelus, whose father Admetus was Pheres' son.
Aethe is Menelaus's mare, whose name means 'fiery'. Antilochus drives Nestor's horses and urges them to overtake her.
A disc's throw is a measure of distance, roughly how far an athlete can hurl the heavy discus.
The doubling-post is the turning-post at the far end of the course, which the chariots must round and return from.
Diomed is called an Aetolian by descent because his father Tydeus came from Aetolia before settling in Argos.
A tripod is a three-legged bronze cauldron stand, a common valuable prize and wager in Homeric society.
The woman and cauldron are Diomed's first prize, set out by Achilles for the winner of the chariot race.
Neleus was Nestor's father, so Antilochus is described by his grandfather's line.
"Not even a dead heat" means that even in a longer race Menelaus's mare would have outright passed Antilochus, not merely tied him.
The son of Admetus is Eumelus, whose chariot crashed earlier in the race after Minerva broke his yoke, so he drags it on foot.
The son of Tydeus is Diomed, who has already won the race and takes first prize.
Antilochus says Eumelus should have prayed; the Greeks believed gods could cause misfortune, and Minerva had in fact wrecked his chariot.
Holding the staff marked the right to speak in assembly; the herald handed it to the speaker.
"Baulked my horses" means obstructed them; Antilochus had forced his horses into a narrow gap, making Menelaus pull back to avoid a collision.
Swearing by Neptune (the Greek Poseidon), god of horses and the sea, was a solemn oath fitting a chariot dispute.
A talent was a measure of weight in gold; the word is used here for a unit of value.
Nestor recalls funeral games for Amarynceus, a king of the Epeans, held at Buprasium in Elis, where he won most events in his youth.
"Vouchsafes" means graciously grants; the winner is the one to whom Apollo gives greater staying power.
Refers to the funeral games held at Thebes for Oedipus, a hero of the Theban legends; Mecisteus's victory there shows Euryalus's boxing heritage.
"Thongs" are leather straps wound around the fists, the ancient boxing glove; "girt" means belted.
"Sea-wrack" is seaweed cast up on shore; "Boreas" is the north wind; "furs" means roughens with ripples.
"Essay" means attempt or try.
"Lift me, or I you" refers to a wrestling hold: lifting the opponent off the ground to throw him; Jove decides the outcome.
"Put not each other further" means do not push each other to further suffering.
A 'measure' (metretes) is a unit of liquid volume; the text only says the bowl was large, holding six of them.
Lycaon, a son of Priam, was captured by Achilles earlier and sold as a slave to Lemnos; Eueneus ransomed him, paying this bowl to Patroclus.
'Essay' means to attempt or try; 'stand forward, you who will essay' is a call for contestants.
The shuttle carries the woof (weft thread) across the warp (lengthwise threads); the weaver draws it close to her chest, so the comparison shows Ulysses almost touching Ajax.
'Offal' here means animal refuse left from the slaughtered cattle, which Ajax slips on.
Antilochus jokes that the gods favour age, since the older men beat him; this is tactful flattery aimed at Achilles.
'Blades' here means swords or spears; the contest is a mock duel to first blood.
A quoit is a heavy disc or lump of metal thrown for distance; 'erewhile' means formerly.
Teucer failed to vow a hecatomb (large sacrifice) to Apollo, god of archers, so Apollo spoiled his aim at the bird.
'Chased' means decorated with engraved or embossed metalwork; 'to wit' means 'that is to say'.

context_notes.text: Thetis is Achilles' sea-goddess mother. She inspires the men's grief, and she will later bring Achilles his new armour.
Washing off blood and filth was normal after battle. Achilles' refusal marks him as a mourner, and the shaved head offered at the pyre was also a mourning custom.
Patroclus predicts Achilles' death at Troy, a fate Achilles already knows is coming.
Peleus is Achilles' father; the golden vase was a gift from Achilles' mother, the sea-goddess Thetis, meant to hold his bones.
Ida is the mountain near Troy, rich in forests and springs, from which the Greeks fetch timber.
Spercheius is a river god of Achilles' homeland, Phthia. Youths grew their hair for a river god and cut it at manhood.
Killing captives at a hero's funeral is human sacrifice, showing Achilles' rage over Patroclus' death.
Venus (the Greek Aphrodite) sides with the Trojans, so she protects the body of Hector.
Iris is the gods' swift messenger, associated with the rainbow.
Oceanus is the great river encircling the world. The Ethiopians lived at its edge and were favored by the gods, who often joined their feasts.
Thrace, north of the Aegean, was the traditional home of the winds, especially Boreas.
Hades is both the god of the dead and the name of the underworld where souls go.
Achilles' immortal horses were a gift from the gods to Peleus. The driver he mourns is Patroclus, whose funeral these games honour.
Phoenix, an old companion of Achilles' father Peleus, serves as umpire, a trusted witness to ensure the race is judged honestly.
Apollo had protected Aeneas, whom Diomed wounded, so he opposes Diomed here; Minerva favours Diomed throughout the poem.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) favours Diomed throughout the Iliad; here she also made Eumelus crash by breaking his yoke.
Idomeneus is the leader of the Cretan contingent and an older, respected warrior.
Achilles is hosting the games in honour of the dead Patroclus and acts as judge of the contest.
Achilles took this breastplate from Asteropaeus, a Trojan ally he killed in battle by the river Xanthus.
Nestor is the aged king of Pylos, Antilochus's father, famous for wisdom and long speeches about his past.
Boxing follows the chariot race; the mule prize is valuable because mules were prized as strong working animals.
The son of Tydeus is Diomedes, who acts as Euryalus's second, his helper in the contest.
The son of Peleus is Achilles, who hosts these funeral games for Patroclus and awards the prizes.
Ajax, son of Telamon, is famed for strength; Ulysses is famed for cleverness. The match pits brawn against cunning.
Ajax son of Oileus, the 'lesser Ajax,' is a different man from Ajax son of Telamon, who appears later.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) favours Ulysses throughout the poem; Ajax son of Oileus was later punished by her in the legends.
Patroclus killed Sarpedon, a Trojan ally, in Book 16 and took his armour.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war; 'of the race of Mars' means descended from him.
Achilles honours Agamemnon without a contest, soothing the tension left from their quarrel earlier in the poem.

literary_notes.text: Achilles' vows of dragging Hector and slaying twelve Trojans foretell the brutal acts later in the book and show his grief turning to vengeance.
The sacrificed animals and streams of blood create a vivid, violent picture suited to a warrior's funeral feast.
"Windy Ilius" uses a stock descriptive phrase for Troy, recalling the chase of Hector and closing the scene on exhaustion.
The ghost's gentle reproach shows Patroclus' loyalty and Achilles' neglect through grief, deepening their bond.
Fate is imagined as a beast with wide jaws that has swallowed Patroclus, making his death feel predatory and inescapable.
The ghost vanishing "as a vapour" conveys its insubstantial nature and Achilles' frustrated longing in a single image.
The foot soldiers are likened to a cloud, conveying their vast number and dark, slow, massed movement.
Achilles addresses the absent river god directly, voicing his bitterness that Peleus' hopes will never be fulfilled.
The lock grown for a homecoming becomes a gift for the dead, since Achilles knows he will never return.
Achilles' threat against Hector's body sets up the gods' intervention, which will contradict his boast.
The winds act as gods with voices, rising with a cry that tears the air, so weather becomes divine action.
Achilles' grief is compared to a father's mourning for a son, showing his love for Patroclus as deep family loss.
"Saffron-mantled Dawn" is a stock Homeric description, giving the sunrise a color and a human figure.
Achilles' mention of his own death, when the bones will be reunited with his, anticipates his fate at Troy.
The grieving horses weep and let their manes trail, mirroring human mourning for Patroclus and deepening Achilles' sorrow.
Nestor compares the woodman and the pilot to the driver, building his argument that skill beats strength.
The dust rising like a cloud or whirlwind conveys the speed and violence of the start.
Minerva answers Apollo's trick by restoring the whip and breaking Eumelus' yoke, showing the gods taking sides in human contests.
Menelaus's angry words show his fairness and his hurt pride, and portray Antilochus as clever and daring but unscrupulous.
The white star on the horse's forehead is compared to the moon, giving a vivid, recognisable detail Idomeneus can spot from afar.
Ajax accuses Idomeneus of laying down the law while doing exactly that himself, and Idomeneus is in fact right about Diomed.
Homer measures the closeness of Menelaus with a precise comparison to a horse's tail brushing the wheel, making the finish tense.
Antilochus's humble, flattering speech shows his quick wit and diplomacy, letting him escape blame and keep the goodwill of his elders.
Menelaus's softened anger is compared to dew falling on ripening corn, an image of refreshment and relief.
The narrator suddenly addresses Menelaus directly, "O Menelaus," which adds warmth and sympathy.
Achilles's gentle gift honours Nestor's age while reminding us of his lost strength, and of Patroclus, who will not be seen again.
Epeus's boasting reveals his arrogance, yet his admission of weakness in war adds a touch of self-awareness.
Euryalus's leap and collapse is compared to a fish flung up by waves onto the seaweed shore, then falling back into the water.
The locked wrestlers are likened to rafters braced together, conveying their firm, balanced, mutual strain.
Ulysses is repeatedly marked by cunning ("full of wiles"), and here his trickery pays off just as the epithet promises.
The weaving comparison turns a domestic scene into an image of how closely Ulysses follows, showing his stamina and cunning.
Ajax's bitter complaint is comic: he is right about Minerva's help, yet he is humiliated by dung.
Comparing the discus throw to a herdsman's flung stick makes Polypoetes' throw look effortless and enormous.
Meriones' prompt vow to Apollo contrasts with Teucer's neglect, showing that piety brings success.
